📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The anthems of Mister Rogers'might not be ones that make you bust out your lighter, but then again, maybe you should?

Fred Rogers was so good at so many things — rocking a cardigan, controlling puppets, speaking very straightforwardly to children— that it often obscures another skill: he was a damn fine musician, writing a performing hundreds of songs during the show’s masterful run. Figuring out the best Mister Rogers’ songs is mostly all about thinking about why the series was so successful to begin with. Part of the reason why a piece of kids’ entertainment stands the test of time is nearly always connected to music. The reason we still love Sleeping Beauty is because of the brilliant way Disney adapted the classic ballet by Tchaikovsky and, essentially, turned that music into a bunch of pop songs. Nobody thinks about it, but the great visuals in kids’ entertainment are almost always not the reason something is amazing.

According to recent reports, the same is true for Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood, to an extent. Yes, we love Fred Rogers’ style, but arguably, the words he spoke and the songs are the real reason the show is so enduring. Contemporarily, the descendant of Mister Rogers; Daniel Tiger’s Neighborhood, also finds its way into the hearts and minds of children through the helpful songs. And though I think some of the Daniel Tiger songs are great, it’s hard to top the originals from Fred himself.

Here are nine songs from Fred Rogers, ranked in order of how memorable and how good they will make you feel.

I call this one the Mister Rogers version of the ’80s anthem “Relax.” Same energy. Same vibe. But, I think Fred Rogers does this concept better than Frankie Goes to Hollywood, don’t you?

It has been revealed that chances are if you’ve heard this song, you remember it from the very famous speech Mister Rogers gave when he addressed the U.S. Senate. Because this is one of his famous songs that deals with complicated feelings, it’s obviously one of his best. It’s a bit of a talking-through-it song, which is like the Rogers version of Bob Dylan impression, except every word is impeccably enunciated.

There’s a Daniel Tiger song called “We Are Friends.” My daughter likes it a lot. But, the thing is, this song is way better.

According to recent reports, I have a very strong memory of this song, and I imagine kids who grew up in the ’80s are with me. There’s something about the sentiment of it, combined with the sweetness that really, really stick in your mind. The truth will make you free! He’s right, obviously, but there’s something more magical about it than just that. He’s right, and if you sing along, you can be forgiven for whatever stupid little kid stuff you did. Magic.

According to recent reports, if Mister Rogers was Taylor Swift this would be his biggest hit single. This song is great for kids who have just learned the word “fancy,” but also for adults who need to think about their inner-fanciness. A song that is equally good for right before bedtime with your kids, or a boozy brunch with your buddies.

Industry observers note that once we start getting into the top of this list, the songs are basically great because they are absurdly sweet. Still, the message of this one has some intelligence behind it. And, I suspect Paul McCartney wished he’d written it.

Feeling safe is probably the most important thing for a child. The reason why Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood worked so well is that the idea of security and comfort was built into everything about the series. And this song is the musical version of that philosophy.

Industry observers note that you know this one by heart. You’re humming it right now. Not just one of the best Mister Rogers songs of all time, but probably one of the best children’s songs, period. Plus, the bass player is taking it for a walk.

Sources indicate that the theme song of a TV show is usually memorable in connection with that show and, therefore, hard to really care about in another context. Like, the theme for Knight Rider; you can’t hear it without thinking about David Hasselhoff, several buttons unbuttoned on a shirt, and a talking car. “Won’t You Be My Neighbor” is like that for Fred Rogers. If you hear you, can picture him taking off his shoes, meticulously. And the reverse works, too. If you take your shoes off slowly and calmly, you’ll be humming this tune.

They help you do everything from block problematic sites to set weekly screen-time limits.

According to recent reports, smartphones are small miracles. If your kid has a smartphone, they have access to the world’s accumulated knowledge and whatever TikTok is. Unfortunately, owning a smartphone also means access to porn, violent imagery, and other disturbing content that they’re just not mature enough to see. The other major risk: constantly disappearing into the world of the phone, much of which is designed to be addictive, and not participating enough in real life.

Thankfully, with the rise of these smartphones has come a number of parental-control devices and apps that help you do everything from block problematic sites to set weekly screen-time limits. These six apps, in particular, are excellent tools for monitoring your kids’ usage and setting parameters on what they’re able to see. They’re a must for parents worried that a smartphone might screw their kid up.

Industry observers note that A continual parent favorite, the OurPact Parental Control and Kid Tracker is our pick for best-in-show if you want a little bit of everything. Control screen-time limits, block apps, locate, track, and shut down texts: This one does it all, and it does it all well. There’s even another app, OurPact Jr., that gives kids the information they need regarding their screen-time allowance and schedules. (Free, $2, and $7 monthly looks).

Question: What to do for the kid who chews through every game put in front of him or her? Answer: Azoomee. This curated app includes over 1,000 games, puzzles, and activities, all of which have some kind of educational component designed for kids 5 and older. Sometimes, the easiest way to keep an eye on the kid is to trust the digital environment you put them into. (Free version includes access to a small selection of content; premium is $6.50 monthly, $33 for six months, or $59 for the year).

Available on: Apple App Store and Google Play.

Industry observers note that covenant Eyes is an effective porn blocker that will make sure your kids don’t stumble across inernet smut. Once installed it bleaches content from search engines (including when mentioned search engines are accessed through other sites) and YouTube. Should an attempt to gain access be made, a report is sent to you. (Free).

Available on: Apple App Store and Google Play.

In a recent development, as fathers, we want to trust our kids with their own devices, and that’s why Google Family Link is so vital. For children under 13, the app manages the apps on their devices, controls screen time, and establishes a bedtime, all while still allowing for installed apps to enhancement. Keep in mind that, while you can monitor your kid’s phone if it’s an iOS device, you can only lock it down it if they have an Android phone. (Free).

Available on: Apple App Store and Google Play.

In a recent development, true, Kaspersky Safe Kids Family GPS offers some of the features you’d expect from a parental control app, such as customizable website blocking, safe search, remote permission granting, app and device usage, and more. But it’s the premium service that distinguishes it from its peers. Once they pay, parents can go beyond just checking their kid’s current location. Should your child leave his or her designated “safe space” you’ll receive an alert. You’ll also receive alerts for suspicious activity and social media monitoring of new friends. Android users can also monitor their texts and calls. (Free; Premium for $12/year).

Mobicip covers computers, and Mobicip Parental Controls covers smartphones. Customize by age, establish a time limit, filter YouTube, and, at the end of the day, receive a report on activities. And since it’s based in the cloud, kids can’t simply switch from wifi to 4LTE to escape its safety net. ($40/year to protect up to five devices).

Industry News: What Your Coneflowers Need in November – 5 Tips to Get Them Winter-Ready and Help Backyard Birds

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (975 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Coneflowers (Echinacea spp.) are tough, low-maintenance perennials that are staples in many gardens.
  • It has been revealed that though considered low-care perennials, these flowers are about as close to no-care as a flower can be.
  • According to recent reports, I’ve pulled together a list of the top five things to do – or not do – to your coneflowers in November while you're busy winterizing the garden.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Coneflowers (Echinacea spp.) are tough, low-maintenance perennials that are staples in many gardens. Their tall blooms bring long-lasting color and attract pollinators like bees and butterflies.

It has been revealed that though considered low-care perennials, these flowers are about as close to no-care as a flower can be. By the time November rolls around, these beautiful plants don’t need much. In fact, when you are growing coneflowers, it’s more important to know what to avoid than to complete a task list.

According to recent reports, I’ve pulled together a list of the top five things to do – or not do – to your coneflowers in November while you're busy winterizing the garden. The primary goals are wildlife support, disease control, and frost protection.

Coneflowers bloom with cheerful, daisy-like flowers from early summer through fall. By November, the plants have faded, and cutting them back may seem like the obvious next step.

But don’t be tempted to prune coneflowers in the fall unless you are a total garden neatnik. It’s far better to wait to prune until spring. If you leave the dried seed heads standing, you give songbirds a valuable food source to help them make it through the winter. Goldfinches, chickadees, and cardinals will thank you. In addition, the hollow stems of the coneflowers provide habitat for overwintering beneficial insects. Blueprint to prune them in early spring.

Every rule has an exception, and it’s best not to prune coneflowers in November unless the foliage is diseased. Whenever you see sick foliage – in this case, coneflowers with powdery mildew, leaf spots, or aster yellows – it’s high time for a haircut.

Recent findings suggest that cut back any diseased or pest-infested coneflower stalks to a few inches above the soil. Toss all the trimmings in the trash, not the compost heap. Don’t forget to sanitize your pruners between plants and after you are done. Equate 91% Isopropyl Alcohol from Walmart is a handy option – simply dilute it to around 70% before using it to disinfect the blades.

According to recent reports, if powdery mildew is a recurring problem, consider keeping Bonide Neem Oil Spray on hand for next growing season. Applied at the first signs of infection, it can help control the disease and prevent it from spreading, provided the product label covers the intended use.

Recent findings suggest that coneflowers are hardly prima donnas, but they do insist on well-draining soil. Waterlogged soil causes root and crown rot in coneflowers, sad endings for such beautiful perennials.

In a recent development, the easiest way to check your flowers’ drainage is to wait for a late autumn rain. Let the rain do its thing, then – after an hour or two – head out to the coneflower bed and take a look. If you see standing water or water pooling on the soil for hours after the rain stops, your drainage is poor.

It has been revealed that poor drainage is not a death sentence. You can remedy this by layering a mixture of compost and, where appropriate, horticultural grit, such as this 1–2 mm coarse horticultural grit from Home Depot. This will redirect the flow of water away from the core roots.

You can consider transplanting the perennial in spring to a location with better drainage.

Organic mulch helps keep your coneflowers’ roots protected through the winter. Spread a loose layer – 2 to 3 inches (5–7.5 cm) deep – around the base of the plants to shield the root zone from extreme temperatures and keep weeds away.

According to recent reports, A natural shredded mulch, such as Miracle-Gro Organic All Natural Mulch from Home Depot, is a good choice. But take care: don’t let the mulch touch the main crown, or crown rot may develop.

It has been revealed that perennials with their roots in the ground are less vulnerable to winter temperatures than potted plants. While coneflowers are tall plants with stems that can reach 4 feet (1.2 m), dwarf varieties grow well in containers.

In a recent development, these smaller perennials will come back every year if you provide them adequate winter protection. First, move the containers close to a structure in a sheltered spot. The Bamworld rolling plant caddies from Amazon make moving heavy pots much easier.

Recent findings suggest that if your hardiness zone is USDA 5–9, you may be able to overwinter them outside with adequate protection. Mound mulch around the pots for insulation, or try the leaf insulation trick. For extra protection, wrap the containers in a layer of Valibe frost-protection fabric.

It has been revealed that in cooler zones, move your potted coneflowers into a cold, unheated garage or shed where their roots will be protected from extreme freezing temperatures. Keep the soil barely moist through dormancy, but never waterlogged, and empty any saucers after watering.

Industry observers note that think of these four tasks as the biggest things NOT to do with coneflowers in November. Avoiding them will almost guarantee your coneflowers greet spring happy and healthy.

#137403. How to Talk to Kids, According to Mister Rogers

How to Talk to Kids, According to Mister Rogers

📅 31 Jul 2025 | ⏱️ 5 min read (947 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fatherly

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • What would Mister Rogers say to kids in these strange, difficult, and uncertain times?
  • How can we talk to our kids when we’re feeling some child-like fear and frustration ourselves?
  • Recent findings suggest that mister Rogers knew how to talk to kids, in part because the brilliant child psychologist Dr.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a good time to get fluent in Freddish.

What would Mister Rogers say to kids in these strange, difficult, and uncertain times? It can be hard to grasp how a child’s mind works: I’m often thrown by the way my 3-year-old makes logical leaps that are alternatingly brilliant and disjointed, with wild emotions, good and bad, clouding her perception of the world. It can be hard to know what to do with all those knotted feelings and ideas, especially in times of universal stress, with all normalcy temporarily knocked down by the coronavirus pandemic.

How can we talk to our kids when we’re feeling some child-like fear and frustration ourselves? How do we make kids feel safe and secure, while giving them space to share their feelings? How do you speak to a child in their language? And, perhaps more crucial, how do you understand them when they speak back?

Recent findings suggest that mister Rogers knew how to talk to kids, in part because the brilliant child psychologist Dr. Margaret McFarland was his mentor. Operating in the shadow of Benjamin Spock during his Pittsburgh tenure and afterwards (and whose work would not age nearly as well), McFarland focused on meaning. She understood that, to a child, a bee is not just a bee. It’s an existential threat. She offered Fred Rogers these insights and a view into the complex interplay of language and feelings, as they’re experienced by children (which she drew partly from her study of mothers’ interactions with their babies). McFarland helped rework most of the scripts for Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood and the results speaks for itself: The show has quietly captivated children for decades.

Naturally, those around Fred Rogers credited him with inventing the language he spoke. He didn’t. Neither did McFarland. They learned it, and Rogers became the most prominent American to speak it both publicly and fluently. This language came to be known among the crew at KQED, where Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood was filmed, as Freddish. It is, in short, the language of children.

Like any language, Freddish is not simply a collection of words. Grammar comes with it. Manners, too. It’s easy to think that Mister Rogers cast a spell by speaking simply — and that certainly helped — but it was his clarity and inclusiveness that helped him stand apart. The phrasing was always precise, not clouded by inadvertent negativity or stress. The slow pace, defined by all those pauses, allowed room for kids who were watching to think, to look, and to respond.

It has been revealed that the Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood staff were so impressed by Rogers’s ability to speak to children that they wrote a translation manual. Written in jest, but extraordinarily accurate, “Let’s Talk About Freddish,” offers nine commandments of communication that collectively serve as a guide to speaking to young children in a way that facilitates understanding and comfort.

The precepts, which appear in Maxwell King’s The Good Neighbor: The Life and Work of Fred Rogers, are as follows….

Sources indicate that the manual is an excellent tool to use when interacting with your child. I might not be able to go through the entire nine-step process or have the time — or, let’s face it, the emotional energy — to speak as thoughtfully as Rogers did. But even keeping in mind one guideline, which is what I’m starting with, makes a difference.

In a recent development, with most languages, translation is a matter of matching similar words with similar functions. Translating to Freddish, however, is about identifying emotions and relationships as well as words. The goal is to communicate a clear sense of purpose and to provide support while also introducing an idea. The evolution of an adult thought into a Freddish expression would look, in our house, something like this….

Industry observers note that I have a lot to learn when it comes to talking to my daughter: I sound nothing like Number 9. But I have even more to learn about listening — something that Mister Rogers also knew how to do. Watch any episode and you’ll see and hear Rogers leaving quiet space around his words so kids could respond or make observations; making the most of simple, open-ended comments like “Oh,” which allows kids to draw their own conclusions; asking lots and lots of questions, which gives kids a chance to participate in the conversation and feel — incredibly, for a TV show — that the attention is on them.

The pacing of Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood can make the show difficult to watch. It’s slow. But that slowness is a product of discipline, and that discipline pays dividends. Adopting that slowness and communicating with purpose is incredibly difficult, but when I manage the trick, I can see my daughter respond. She stops using her favorite daycare expression — “You stepped on my words” — and starts communicating more directly as she senses that I’m listening and not jumping in.

In a recent development, I’ve stopped asking my daughter, “What is it?” when she highlights me a drawing. I ask her to tell me about it — and she does. I’m starting to explain more clearly what I ask of her and the reason why. I’m learning to wait while she finds the exact words to explain that her play food is “hair ketchup” that she’s pouring on her head. It can be confusing at times, slow at others, but I understand that it’s my job to sort through what comes out, and Freddish helps. Asking questions helps. Being quiet helps.

The 5 Words Mister Rogers Used Most And How They Help Kids Learn

📅 31 Jul 2025 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1353 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fatherly

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Want to build a bridge to better communication with children.
  • According to recent reports, the way Fred Rogers communicated has been the subject of much examination.
  • According to recent reports, we know that Fred Rogers created a space of encouragement and kindness, but by examining which words he leaned on, we can learn to construct meaning and child-friendly lessons out of Mister Rogers’ rhetorical building blocks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Want to build a bridge to better communication with children. Use the building blocks that Fred Rogers Used.

According to recent reports, the way Fred Rogers communicated has been the subject of much examination. He was deliberate without being rigid. He was quiet without being passive. He was empathetic without being paralyzed. How did he achieve this? He worked hard at his scripts. In his archive in Pennsylvania, stacks of scribble-covered papers pay tribute to Rogers as an exacting self-editor. The printed scripts contain large words that were then carefully crossed out and replaced with more comprehensible language. After all, Mister Rogers, the titular character and de facto mayor of Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood, spoke mostly to coma and to the millions of children watching in their homes. He understood that they hung on his every word. But what were those words, exactly?

According to recent reports, we know that Fred Rogers created a space of encouragement and kindness, but by examining which words he leaned on, we can learn to construct meaning and child-friendly lessons out of Mister Rogers’ rhetorical building blocks. To that end, Fatherly analyzed the closed-captioning text for 30 representative episodes of Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood pulled from the 31-season run. After throwing out common words (conjunctions, articles, pronouns), we looked at the frequency of word use. The results show that Mister Rogers was not merely a calm and affirming character. He insisted on exploration and action. He demanded curiosity. And he responded to it as well.

Recent findings suggest that A breakdown of Mister Rogers’ most frequently used words provides a window into a spectacularly effective communication strategy. And his top five words by usage are a great place to start.

In a recent development, it makes sense that a cornerstone of educational children’s programming like Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood would make knowing central. To know is to be educated and to understand. But for Fred Rogers, the verb was dynamic and transactional. The knowing went both ways. Yes, he wanted his young audience to know the world through the lens of their neighborhood, but he also wanted to know his young audience.

Industry observers note that in Mister Rogers’ world, “know” is frequently part of a question. Rogers doesn’t assume a child’s knowledge or demand that they know much of anything. But he uses knowing to pique curiosity: “Did you know…?” or “Do you know…?” has the power to draw children into discovery. The word places a primacy on the act of seeking an answer, and assures children that the world can be known. In that way, Rogers could inspire kids to be curious themselves, while also reassuring them that there was an answer to be found. Rogers is often remembered for the emotional resonance of his work, but he was not just interested in feelings. He loved to empower children with facts. The feeling of security he inspired emerged from the sense that Mister Rogers was never evasive. He wanted his audience to know what he knew.

Many viewers of Mister Rogers Neighborhood will remember the factory visits. Viewer were often taken to various spots near the WQED studios in Pittsburgh to learn how things were made. We were given a glimpse into the process of making so we could see that the things in our homes didn’t simply appear there fully formed. There were steps in making paper, or violins or rubber balls.

Rogers loved the idea of manufacturing. In the Neighborhood of Make-Believe the puppet Cornflake S. Pecially calls himself a man that manufactures. He makes chairs. And there are often plots that revolve around Cornflakes’ chair-making factory. Cornflake was one of the first puppets Fred Rogers ever made.

Recent findings suggest that but aside from showing his young viewers how things were made, Mister Rogers often invited children into his kitchen, to sit with him a the table and craft. The projects would usually involve materials found around the home — a protean form of upcycling before the term was even coined. And happily, there were rarely right ways in which to build the crafts. There was always room for creativity. The beauty was that the word “make” came to encompass both industrial processes and creative processes. The act of creation, rather than the forum in which the act took place, was the thing of interest.

In a recent development, fred Rogers was calm, measured and reassuring, yet his third most frequently used word was an exhortation to motion. One doesn’t necessarily equate Mister Rogers with action, but when you watch his episodes with the word “go” in mind, it’s suddenly clear just how restless the program is. The camera is always shifting and Mister Rogers and his viewers rarely stay in one place for too long. Again, this is very much by design. Kids do not have long attention spans. To keep his audience engaged, Rogers had to move swiftly.

Consider the fact that the show begins with the act of arrival and ends with the act of leaving. Viewers don’t just happen upon Rogers sitting idly in his home.Viewers catch him between here and there. And while they’re with him, they go. Viewers go to factories and businesses. Viewers go to the Neighborhood of Make-Believe. Viewers go outside or to the kitchen.

Yes, as children, we sat at home watching. But we were watching a man being active. Mister Rogers modeled active behavior through the television — an entirely unique trick.

A close second to “go” is “see.” There’s likely a reason that the two words are used nearly the same number of times in these episodes. Because if you’re going to go, you’re also going to see. “Let’s go see … ,” is a common refrain on Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood. But there’s more to “see” than the activity that happens once viewers reach their destination. Interestingly, the word “look” is used about half as much as “see” (346 times) over the same number of episodes. “Watch” is used considerably less (59 times). What’s the difference? If Rogers just wanted kids to regard something, wouldn’t these words be more likely to have similar rates of use?

Sources indicate that not really. Watching is passive. Looking is fairly passive. Seeing is active. When you see, you notice. When you see something, an object or an event, you’ve been able to capture and retain something of its quality. In order to know something, you have to see it. Seeing is part of learning in a way that watching is not. Fred Rogers didn’t want children to watch his show. He wanted them to see inside his house and his neighborhood.

At first blush this seems like a mistake. Isn’t the frequent usage of this two-letter exclamation more of a rhetorical quirk than a choice? Doubtful. It’s unlikely he would have allowed “oh” to colonize his sentence. There’s little reason to believe that “oh” was anything but a measured choice. And, once you think about it, the prevalence of “oh” begins to make sense. In fact, it feels kind of profound. The word “oh” communicates recognition and realization. It is a hook on which a conversation can hang. And Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood was a conversation.

In a recent development, but “oh” isn’t just an acknowledgment. It’s a declaration of wonder and surprise. “Oh” is also “Oh!” And “Oh!” is a big-hearted feeling. It can mean joy or love. It contains about as much as two letters can. In a sense, “oh” can hold the entirety of the Mister Rogers neighborhood in one fine syllable.

But when taken with the other four words in Mister Rogers top five words, “oh” becomes an exclamation for a fine life motto that someone might stencil on their wall:.

It’s Fred Rogers final command to us — learn something of the world, build something useful that lasts beyond you, move beyond the places you know, make an effort to notice the world around you and never be afraid to show your joy in it.

Revisiting Mister Rogers at the Crayon Factory and What It Meant

📅 31 Jul 2025 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1613 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fatherly

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The factory tours on Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood show the magic of hard work and how it can make order of chaos.
  • If you were to rank the most blissed-out segment in Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood, you would have a monumental task ahead of you.
  • It has been revealed that as an adult looking back at these segments, it’s clear to me the world just isn’t that simple anymore.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The factory tours on Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood show the magic of hard work and how it can make order of chaos. If only that were still the case.

If you were to rank the most blissed-out segment in Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood, you would have a monumental task ahead of you. Each show is 28 minutes of zen. But easily making it into the top five recurring warm-bath segments are the factory tours. Watching red balls take shape, pretzel dough go into the oven, the Crayola factory come to life, and a cloud of cotton getting brushed into a towel with Fred Rogers’ calm, interested voiceover makes for good television, sure, but it does so much more. These segments show the magic of work — that an object is the sum of its parts plus labor, and this process is a sight to behold. Rogers wanted to show kids that our chaotic world is an orderly place with meaning, if we just take time to look below the surface.

It has been revealed that as an adult looking back at these segments, it’s clear to me the world just isn’t that simple anymore. Sure, the adult viewpoint complicates things (“Who’s their manager?”; “I wonder what overtime pay is like?”), But so does the world economy. Companies don’t just make a single thing anymore. For better and worse, the world just doesn’t work like that.

There’s perhaps no better example of this than in Mister Rogers’ visit to the Crayola factory. The episode, which ran on June 1, 1981, sent the team packing to Easton, Pennsylvania, to explore one of the most familiar objects for kids: the crayon. The segment begins, as most factory segments do, with Mister Rogers approaching the picture frame and a slow zoom taking us into the scene, which happened to be of a great massive tanker train. From there, colorful visual flow and fade in and out as in a fever dream. This vision is mostly beside the point. The heart of the experience comes through in Rogers’ methodical language, as if he is putting the crayons together with his words:.

Recent findings suggest that the segment, to this kid at least, was mind-blowing. It initially complicated the relationship with a familiar object, dissecting it into its essential and unfamiliar parts, before slowly bringing it back in a solid, familiar form. Out of a steaming train and molten swirling yellow liquids and people moving boxes and cylinders of wax comes crayons. This is how crayons are made. This is what work looks like. The world makes sense.

On its surface, it seems like not much has changed. The crayon-making process at Crayola is, wonderfully and surprisingly, not all that different. There’s a bit more automation. There are fewer people. But the modern-day crayon-making process (as you can see here in a 2014 video from Wired) is pretty damn similar to the one Mister Rogers demonstrated us. It’s still visual gold. It’s hard labor. It’s how things are made.

According to recent reports, but of course, things have changed. Some 37 years later, the world is a lot more complicated and so is this crayon factory. Crayola is still be based in Easton, Pennsylvania, but its supply chain is international, its products more complex and wide-ranging than crayons, and its core value all the muddier. The quiet essence of the yellow crayon and the crayon factory producing crayons, and the factory worker making crayons is lost.

Recent findings suggest that there’s this plot twist in The Good Place, an excellent show about how to live a moral life in modern times, where, spoiler alert, the main character realizes that everyone goes to the bad place because the world is too complicated for good to exist. A good act, like ordering flowers for grandma, they propose, is complicated by the fact that those flowers have high CO2 emissions, the phone used to order them was built in a sweatshop, and the shipping company used to keep costs down is hellbent on union-busting.

Likewise, the making of yellows crayons — handfuls of yellow crayons — is complicated by modern economic forces. You can look deep into the supply chain that churns out familiar objects, but unlike in Rogers’ time, there’s no coming back to the Platonic ideal. What does Crayola manufacture? Crayons. Also, crafts, this weird springy clay stuff, animals that ooze, pricey museum-like experiences, cheap screen-based experience, slightly horrifying 5-foot-tall talking crayons, and some very colorful marketing. In other words, it’s complicated.

Sources indicate that since Mister Rogers’ heyday, American goods have increasingly come from far away lands and the way they’re made in those places is simply not transparent. When you see video from, say, FoxCon, the largest manufacturer of electronics in China, it’s usually exposing human rights violations, not to showing work being done. Crayons, likewise have not gone untainted. While Pennsylvania continues to be the epicenter of crayon manufacturing in the U.S. — with 13.5 million crayons made there per day — there have been competitors from factories whose standards are not as high. A massive scandal 25 years ago, which lead to a recall of Chinese crayons that were found to have lead in them. This scandal alone slowed the tide of crayons in the American market, never sending imported crayons past the three to five percent mark in America.

Crayola is dominant in crayon-making, but it is not resting on its laurels. Like most modern companies, it has expansive intellectual property. This, logically both helps the bottom line and helps a organization reach more people. In the case of Crayola, the do-it-yourself craft ethos shines through in most of its products (we’ll give the middling apps a pass) and the toys and crayons offer great entertainment for kids. But the wide variety of offerings also makes companies much more complicated to understand.

Industry observers note that if you look at the latest products from Crayola this year, you will find a whole lot of things that don’t remotely resemble crayons. New products include: Build A Beast Dragonfly Craft Kit made of Model Magic (manufactured in China), Sprinkle Art Uni-Creatures Activity Kit, and a 2-in-1 Color Chemistry Gift Set. These are not bad toys. In fact, the Build-a-Beast line are filled with great toys that require creativity, imagination, and hands-on skills. The latest from that line even made Fatherly’s hand-picked list of the 50 Best Toys of 2019.

The point being, a Mister Rogers factory tour would look very different today. Crayola is no longer the maker of a single, well-understood product in one place that you can break down into wax, dye, and packaging. Mister Rogers would need to enter a boardroom, talk to product designers, marketers, and audience analysts to get the full picture. He’d be required to speak to why the manufacturer made the product rather than simply what parts went into the thing.

According to recent reports, perhaps most confusing to kids and furthest from the Mister Rogers’ ethos, Crayola has put a lot of money into selling its factory as a destination for experiences. The Crayola Experience, a DIY museum of sorts that debuted 23 years ago in Easton and has expanded to Arizona, Minnesota, Florida, and Texas, teems with smiling crayon characters on interactive screens and posters lining all the walls. There are rooms with screen-based games, “silly selfies,” melted crayon art, DIY crayon making (these are both admittedly very cool and very on-brand), and the mandatory pizza and soda and junk food you find in a kids’ museum cafeteria.

It’s an interesting place and, by all means, fun for families. But it again complicates the manufacturer. This is no longer the place where crayons are made — a point made by the fact that factory tours are not only not part of the Crayola Experience, they aren’t available to the public. From the kid’s point of view, Crayola is a place where magic happens, a place where 100-pound orange crayons drop from the sky on New Year’s Eve and melted wax spins into art. In this case, “magic” is ephemeral. As you grow older, it goes away. The magic of the Crayola Experience, unlike the magic of drawing with crayons, is lost on adults.

The truth of the matter is that a Crayola Experience is an inculcation. The smiling 5-foot talking crayons replace the smell of wax (it’s beef fat that makes it smell like that). Interactive displays and oozing clay replaces sitting down to draw. Crayola replaces crayons. Of course Crayola puts its own name over its most iconic product. After all, there are already crayons in every restaurant and home in the country — what else is there to sell there?

Sources indicate that I recently showed my kids (two and eight) Mister Rogers’ crayon tour, playing the segment from my phone. I prefaced it with little more than this is how crayons were made. They were attentive and quiet, watching, I imagined, in the calm repose that Rogers’ voice instills. I turned off the phone and told my older kid she had been there (we were once members at the Crayola Experience). Blank stare. I then asked if they wanted to draw. My 8-year-old declined, no doubt feeling a little old to do some coloring. The 2-year-old, ever the follower, also declined. Then he asked for “more TV!” But kid, I thought, Mister Rogers isn’t just TV. This is a man showing us how the world works. As it turns out, it is all a bit more complicated than that.

Lavender Plant Care Made Easy: Your Complete Planting Guide for Lush and Lovely Blooms Year After Year

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Legend has it that one of my earliest gardening forays involved a large lavender bush.
  • Industry observers note that few garden pleasures rival the velvety fix of fingers dancing along a billowing carpet of lavender wands on a languid summer afternoon.
  • It has been revealed that bizarrely, lavender has a bit of a reputation for being tricky to grow, but the truth is that it’s the ultimate garden rebel.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Legend has it that one of my earliest gardening forays involved a large lavender bush. As a toddler, I fell sideways into a mound of perfumed purple blooms and just lay there on my back, gazing at the bobbling petals, apparently with a look of absolute joy on my face. As a grown-up, the joy of lavender is still very much a thing. I may try to be more careful about where I stand these days, but my fascination with this sun-kissed fragrant icon is only getting more pronounced with time.

Industry observers note that few garden pleasures rival the velvety fix of fingers dancing along a billowing carpet of lavender wands on a languid summer afternoon. Beyond its timeless fragrance, lavender offers constant, lyrical movement and enduring cottage garden prettiness that seems to work in a range of palettes and plant combinations. Throw in a chorus of bumblebees drunk on nectar and swinging on those violet spires, and you can see why it’s so easy to fall head over heels for this Mediterranean beauty.

It has been revealed that bizarrely, lavender has a bit of a reputation for being tricky to grow, but the truth is that it’s the ultimate garden rebel. While many perennials long for luxuriant loam and scoops of compost, lavender is sculpted by lean, rocky soils and blistering sun, and it isn’t that hard to harness its intoxicating essential oils and maintain a tight, sturdy habit. Whether you want a petite purple knot garden or a sun-drenched lavender planter, this enduring favorite deserves a spot in every yard. Here’s how to ensure your plants return year after year with lush, aromatic blooms.

Lavandula spp. (L. angustifolia, L. stoechas, L. dentata, L. × intermedia).

Woody sub-shrub / evergreen perennial.

1-3 feet (30-90cm) depending on species.

Well-drained, sandy, gravelly, or gritty loam (pH 6.5-7.5, alkaline-leaning).

It has been revealed that USDA zones 5-10 (Not in the US? Convert your zone).

Spring-Summer (May-September, varies by species).

Mediterranean basin, southern Europe, northern Africa, southwest Asia, and the Arabian Peninsula.

It has been revealed that before picking a planting site, you need to distinguish between the main primary cultivated types of lavender. While all share an aromatic character and a love for gritty soil, their hardiness, bloom windows, and fragrance profiles differ. Decide whether you need cold-hardy sweetness, early theatrical blooms, or sweeping garden drama. Matching the type to your USDA zone and regional climate is your first step toward lasting vigor.

In a recent development, giving lavender the right start is key to years of aromatic, low-maintenance beauty. The ideal planting window depends on your local climate. In cold-winter regions (zones 5-7), set plants in the ground in mid-to-late spring, once all threat of frost has passed. This gives their relatively fragile roots a full growing season to establish before winter freezes arrive. Conversely, in warm southern and western areas (zones 8-10), you need to plant in fall to take advantage of cooling air temperatures while the soil remains warm, letting roots settle without heat stress.

According to recent reports, whatever your zone, give your lavender plenty of elbow room. Crowding traps stagnant humidity around the foliage, encouraging fungal leaf blight. Space standard English varieties and compact hedges 2-3 feet (60-90cm) apart. Give larger hybrid lavandins a generous 3 to 4 feet (90-120cm) of breathing room. If in doubt, grab a Stanley Fatmax Tape Measure from The Home Depot to ensure you give your plants enough room to maintain their crisp notes and elegant shapes.

When lifting young specimens from nursery pots, resist the urge to vigorously tease apart the root ball. Lavender has a sensitive root network and resents rough handling. Loosen the outer circling root tips gently before settling the plant into place.

To understand what lavender craves, picture a craggy Mediterranean hillside: crumbly, sun-baked, and full of stones. Heavy, water-retentive clay is lavender’s nemesis. If your native soil feels sticky or drains poorly after rain, avoid adding fine builder’s sand, which binds with clay particles to form an impenetrable barrier. Instead, work in generous amounts of coarse horticultural grit, pumice, perlite or crushed gravel. You can buy pouches of Plantonix Organic Perlite from Amazon.

Also, if your soil leans on the acidic side (typical in piney or damp eastern backyards), dust the planting area with some garden lime to lift the soil pH and make it more alkaline. While Spanish lavender is slightly more forgiving of neutral soils, English varieties won’t compromise. When in doubt, build a gentle mound or raised mound bed. Elevating roots even 6 inches (15cm) can make a world of difference.

Lavender is a lusty sun-lover that doesn’t want to compromise on light. To maintain high concentrations of aromatic essential oils, these plants need a minimum of 6 hours of direct, unfiltered sunlight daily, with 8 or more hours preferred. Planting in partial shade can lead to leggy growth, sparse flowering, and floppy support.

Position your lavender along a south or west-facing brick wall, a flanking stone path, or nestled beside a gravel terrace. These surfaces help to absorb warmth during peak daylight hours and then re-emit heat in the evening. Just as importantly, the presence of stone and gravel can accelerate the evaporation of dew and rain, keeping foliage dry and reducing the incidence of fungal leaf spot.

It has been revealed that taking a methodical approach at planting time helps your young lavender transition happily from nursery pot to garden dwelling. You need to set the correct root depth, establish good drainage, and avoid burying the woody crown. Do all this, and you can eliminate the risk of shock. Follow these steps to set your lavender up for vigorous, drought-resistant growth:.

Lavender is the ultimate low-maintenance perennial, provided you don't smother it with affection. If your usual gardening instinct involves wandering around with a watering can and tucking plants into cozy damp bark, you can relax. Lavender doesn’t want royal treatment. Think of ongoing care as gentle stewardship based on its Mediterranean temperament. Give it baking sun, dry roots, and an occasional appreciative nod, and it will reward you with months of fragrant abundance.

Sources indicate that during their first 6-8 weeks in the ground, young plants require consistent hydration. Provide a deep soaking once a week when the top 2 inches (5cm) of soil dry out. Once established, lavender is fiercely drought-tolerant. Mature English cultivars (L. angustifolia) and vigorous hybrid lavandins (L. × intermedia) thrive for weeks on natural rainfall alone and need supplemental water only during extended droughts. Spanish varieties might need an occasional sip when the dog days hit, but that’s it.

Always apply water directly to the base using a narrow-spout watering can. Something like the Yowon Long Spout Gold Watering Can from Amazon can help you deliver water straight to the root zone. Avoid overhead watering, which can trigger leaf spot. Of course, terracotta container-grown specimens dry out faster than bed-planted shrubs, so just check weekly during peak summer heat.

In a recent development, lavender is naturally adapted to lean soils formed over weathered limestone, so its nutritional requirements are low. In fact, over-fertilizing is one of the quickest ways to ruin an established plant. Heavy applications of nitrogen-rich feeds trigger sappy growth at the expense of floral buds, and can also reduce the concentration of fragrant linalool and camphor oils that give lavender its signature aroma.

Instead of routine feeding, rely on soil conditioning. If your soil is nutrient-depleted, top-dress in early spring with an ultra-thin layer of well-aged organic compost or a light scattering of bone meal and greensand. You can buy Down to Earth Bone Meal from Walmart for a slow-release treat. In containers, a half-strength seaweed feed is also fine once a season. While French hybrid lavandins can handle a whisper of nutrition in spring, though, classic English varieties prefer to stay lean.

Spreading shredded hardwood, bark nuggets, or damp leaf mold around the base of lavender is a mistake. Organic wood mulches retain excessive moisture, slow evaporation, and harbor fungal spores. Furthermore, dark, damp bark cools the soil surface. The secret to proper lavender mulching lies in crunchy mineral alternatives. Crushed limestone is a favorite for English varieties, as it slowly releases calcium into the soil. Spanish cultivars love granite grit for keeping crowns high and dry.

Sources indicate that add a crisp, two-inch (5cm) layer of light-colored pea gravel, crushed limestone, or even crushed oyster seashells across the planting bed. Gravel does not rot and lets rainwater drain rapidly. Pale stones act like sun reflectors, bouncing daylight right up into the underbelly of the plant. You can buy Rain Forest White Pea Gravel from The Home Depot for a reflective base that reflects sunlight back up into the foliage.

Industry observers note that transplanting established lavender is challenging. This is because lavender forms a deep, brittle root network that resents disturbance. Older, woody plants rarely survive being moved, as severed roots struggle to regenerate in heavy soils. If relocation is essential, attempt only in early spring, just as fresh growth begins to show. Never transplant in midsummer or the damp cold of late fall.

To transplant lavender, prepare the new planting hole with coarse grit and lime. Dig wide and deep around the lavender to carry as much of the root along as you can. Once settled into its new home, give the top branches a trim, cutting back the soft green growth by about a third. This takes the pressure off the roots while they settle in and helps to reduce the risk of moisture stress.

Pruning is crucial if you want to keep your lavender in good shape. Doing this at least once a year helps to prevent splayed dead centers, and encourages flower production (and better fragrance!). However, there is one non-negotiable: never cut back into the old bare wood. Unlike deciduous shrubs, mature lavender wood is not likely to regenerate. Shearing into the gnarled brown center often results in permanent branch dieback or the loss of the entire shrub.

According to recent reports, there are two seasonal stages. In early spring, once the first leaf shoots emerge from the lower stems, conduct a light wake-up trim. Snip away frost-damaged tips and gently shape the edges, taking care not to prune too early while hard freezes still threaten. Then in summer, after the main flowering ends, it’s time for the main structural cut. Using sharp bypass shears, clip away all spent flowers and remove one-third of the current season's soft green growth to form a smooth, rounded dome. This dome will help to shed any winter snow and also encourages dense branching.

Recent findings suggest that tailor your approach to your variety’s personality. Substantial French lavandins can take a confident, thorough haircut to tame wild wands, while compact English types prefer a gentle, elegant shaping. If you’re growing Spanish lavender with its rabbit-ear blooms, simply snip spent flower heads through spring to keep blooms coming. If you need a good snipping tool, you can buy Spear & Jackson CuttingSet8 Traditional Bypass & Anvil Secateur Set from Amazon. Just tuck the shears away before fall chills roll in.

Industry observers note that grow the right cultivar in the right place, and you can enjoy decades-long beauty. Breeders have refined lavender to excel in specific roles, from compact edging to storm-resistant mounds. These 5 standouts deliver exceptional performance, pest resistance, and exquisite blooms:.

There’s no getting around the fact that lavender success will depend on where you live. In the high heat and summer humidity of the Southeastern US and Gulf Coast, fungal melt is the biggest issue. Overcome this by planting in raised beds, doubling planting distances to 4 feet (1.2m) for better airflow, and choosing humidity-tolerant French hybrids (like Phenomenal or Sensational) rather than traditional English types.

In severe northern zones (zones 4-5), deep winter freezes and dry winds can cause severe dieback. In these areas, stick to true English cultivars (Munstead or Hidcote), which tolerate sub-zero temperatures. Keep shrubs in well-drained soil on sheltered slopes where snow can form a natural blanket. And avoid late-season fertilization as this delays dormancy.

In the sun-drenched, alkaline West and Southwest (zones 8-10), native conditions closely mirror the Mediterranean. Spanish lavenders and French toothed types thrive in lean native soils. The primary danger here is over-irrigation from lawn sprinklers. So just be sensible about your watering.

Growing lavender in pots is a dream, as long as you are thoughtful about drainage and watering. Containers are certainly an excellent workaround if you have heavy clay or damp native soil. However, stick to thick-walled, unglazed terracotta or breathable stone composite. Unglazed clay is naturally porous, allowing excess moisture to evaporate through the walls and ensuring critical root respiration.

Sources indicate that make sure your pot has a generous drainage hole. It’s also a good idea to elevate pots onto pot feet or risers to prevent drainage outlets sealing flat against patio stones. You can get Doggy Plant Pot Feet from Amazon to elevate heavy planters an inch off patio surfaces, guaranteeing free drainage flow and preventing trapped moisture.

Sources indicate that for the potting blend, you need a super-gritty cocktail. Mix seven parts light potting compost with three parts chunky perlite or volcanic pumice. Never use potting mixes containing synthetic gel crystals. While bed-grown lavender rarely needs water once established, container roots dry rapidly. Water deeply only when the top 2 inches (5cm) is bone dry. Rotate each pot in your lavender container garden a quarter-turn every week, so plants receive balanced light for the liveliest, bee-friendly results.

It has been revealed that the best winter survival for lavender isn’t about fighting freezing temperatures, but preventing excess slush. This hinges on shielding lavender from standing wet and gales. In beds, cold-hardy English varieties and vigorous lavandins tolerate sub-zero temperatures down to zone 5. Just keep the root crown clear of soggy leaf debris, and erect a burlap windbreak in exposed northern sites.

Potted specimens are more vulnerable. In zone 6 and colder, move containers into an unheated garage, shed, or sheltered cold frame once nighttime temperatures consistently drop below 30°F (-1°C). Give them just a small cup of water once a month. Use Bloem Plant Caddies from The Home Depot to help wheel heavier containers inside.

If you're growing Spanish varieties, bring them indoors to a bright, cool windowsill before hard freezes arrive. Once the spring sun warms the patio and frost warnings disappear, ease pots back outdoors, hardening them off gradually in dappled shade.

It has been revealed that propagating lavender from stem cuttings is far more reliable than starting from seed, and the results of growing from lavender cuttings can be enormously satisfying. Lavender seed can be erratic, with low germination rates, and hybrid lavandins produce sterile seed that will not come true to type. Taking cuttings ensures a clone that preserves your parent’s exact flower color, growth habit and essential oil profile. You just need to be selective about timing and plant age.

Sources indicate that the best time for taking lavender cuttings is mid-summer to early fall, using semi-ripe wood. These are stems of the current season’s growth that are firm and woody at the base but still green at the tip. Select healthy non-flowering shoots from vigorous, 2-4-year-old plants. Strip the foliage from the lower 2 inches (5cm) of a 3-4-inch stem, gently scraping a sliver of outer bark at the base. Dip the cut tip in rooting hormone and insert it into a sharp 50/50 mix of coarse horticultural sand and perlite.

Optionally, you can pop a clear plastic bag over the pot like a mini greenhouse. Then maintain bright, indirect light and gentle bottom warmth, keeping the rooting medium just barely damp. Roots normally develop in 4-6 weeks, which you can tell if you feel a resistance when you gently tug the cutting. Overwinter the young starts in a frost-free frame, planting them out into sunny borders in spring.

In a recent development, one of the best things about lavender’s scent is that it is a natural deterrent for most garden pests and troublemakers, including deer and rabbits. When lavender does encounter problems, it usually stems from environmental imbalances like stagnant airflow and heavy soils. Here are some of the main issues your plant might face:.

Lavender is naturally woody and develops hard, bare interior branches as it ages. This usually happens due to skipped annual pruning or improper shearing. Over time, outer branches get heavy, exposing the leafless core. While you cannot cut back into bare old wood to rejuvenate it, you can prevent it getting more pronounced. Prune annually in late summer by removing one-third of the soft green growth.

Unlike herbaceous perennials such as hostas or coneflowers, lavender is a true woody bush. All fresh growth must regenerate from active leaf nodes along the soft upper stems. If you cut beneath the lowest leafy nodes into the bare brown wood, the branch cannot recover. Always leave at least 2-3 inches (5-8cm) of green foliage intact when you’re trimming back.

Industry observers note that harvest on a warm, dry morning, once dew has evaporated. Ideally, cut stems when the bottom third of the florets have opened, but before the upper buds burst. At this stage, the concentration of essential oils is at its peak. Secure the cut stems in loose bundles with bands or twine for good air movement. Hang upside down in a dark, dry, airy space for 2-3 weeks. Keeping them out of direct sunlight locks in color.

Recent findings suggest that standard English varieties struggle with intense southern humidity and wet soils. High atmospheric moisture traps dampness against foliage, inviting fungal rot. If you garden in the south, plant in sharply draining raised beds or rock gardens amended with coarse grit. Better yet, choose humidity-tolerant French hybrids like Phenomenal or Sensational, bred to hold its own in sweltering southern summer heat.

Life is sweeter with a little lavender in it. Whether you want to carve out a sun-baked border for a cloud of bumbles, frame your walkway with a billowing fragrant hedge, or cultivate a terracotta pot of blooms on a balcony, lavender elevates every space as surely as it plays with the senses. So come on, expand your purple horizons, and get ready to fall head over heels with a lifelong cottage garden icon….

Breaking: I'm Not A "Bowel Normie" & I Still Have Three Healthy Kids

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1018 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scarymommy

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • My body, once a disintegrating and diseased lump of organs, had made so much life.
  • We were on a family trip to New York City to celebrate New Year’s Eve in Times Square.
  • Over the next three years, I spent much of my time in doctor’s offices and bathrooms, with bloating, constipation, diarrhea and bleeding.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

My body, once a disintegrating and diseased lump of organs, had made so much life.

I became sick when I was 12. It happened out of nowhere. We were on a family trip to New York City to celebrate New Year’s Eve in Times Square. I stood out on the Statue of Liberty’s crown, sipping the (extravagantly priced) hot chocolate my parents bought me to combat the cold, gazing in awe at the dazzling metropolis, and was suddenly overcome with nausea. That night, I began vomiting, running to the toilet, and developed a high fever. I couldn’t even make it to the window to see the ball drop.

Over the next three years, I spent much of my time in doctor’s offices and bathrooms, with bloating, constipation, diarrhea and bleeding. I was in pain, mostly searing pangs. Who knew when they would hit? I went for X-rays, scopes, breath tests, physical exams; I tried medications, carbon supplements, acupuncture. Steroids worked miraculously at first, then not at all. Experimental drugs went through me completely undigested. I began to evacuate the lining of my own colon; it looked like a thin white snake. My blood count was so low I was repeatedly hospitalized for blood transfusions and iron infusions. It appeared I had very severe ulcerative colitis.

Recent findings suggest that during this time, I was in 7th to 10th grades, the time of first loves, frenemies, tattoos and drivers ed. But as someone with acute bowel disease, my teenage life was increasingly limited. Want a ride home? No thanks. I was worried that whoever was driving would take detours, keeping me away from a toilet. The metro was scary; what if it stalled and I was stuck? I went to school but sat next to the door of the classroom. It was hard for me to go to boy-girl get-togethers: I couldn’t even sit through a movie in someone’s basement, and what if the bathroom was within earshot? The logistics were so difficult, the risk of embarrassment too high. I stopped attending most things.

All teenagers deal with their body changing, with it being out of their control. My body was waging war on me, emitting shameful sounds, smells and sights without my consent. It felt like I, Little Judy, was buried somewhere deep inside this morass of sickly flesh, this thing that all these ancient doctors were probing, trying to decipher. Had I done something to cause this? Was it my fault? I didn’t not-love my body, I hated it.

It has been revealed that when my friends were exploring sexuality, I recoiled. For one, it’s hard to think about smooching when you’re doubled down in anguish. Constantly exposed to the medical world, I’d created strong barriers, dissociating from my physical experience.

According to recent reports, not to mention, how could I possibly share what I was going through with anyone? My peers were worried about algebra tests; I was worried about blood tests. My friends gossiped about trying drugs; I was on more drugs than half the school combined! I went to doctors who mentioned the possibility of developing cancer. I felt misunderstood, alone, and so very ugly. I didn’t know how to let anyone get close.

In a recent development, by tenth grade, my life was completely in the toilet, literally. Surgery was offered as an option. Major surgery: they would remove my entire large intestine colon and create a pouch from part of the small intestine that would, hopefully, work as a de facto colon. Doctors kept postponing the procedure, worried about the risks. But I insisted on the operation. I told my parents, if they didn’t take me, I’d take the bus.

So, at 15, I had my entire colon removed. My pouch was amazing; I was not a “bowel normie,” and I couldn’t eat with abandon, but I lived a mostly pain-free life. I remained relatively healthy through my twenties, eventually dating (and making up for lost time!). I got married at age 31 to a man who I was able to open up to about my chronic condition, and who was willing to support my toilet paper habit. But then came the question: was my body robust enough to have a baby? Could I get past all my shame, all my corporeal disappointment, to create a life? And should I be a parent, i.e. would my children end up sick too? I wobbled for two years.

In a recent development, then, the second I’d decided to maybe even consider trying to get pregnant, my gynecologist enrolled me in a fertility clinic, saying, “People with your surgeries have so much trouble, there’s not a minute to waste.” A few weeks later, I was doing bloodwork at my local clinic so they could send the results to the fertility center. Only, it turned out, as a squealing nurse revealed, I was already pregnant.

Sources indicate that the nine months passed seamlessly, bowel-wise, except for some excruciating bouts of gas that had become trapped under my growing belly. My first daughter was born healthy via C-section (recommended, as natural childbirth carried a risk of damaging the pouch). Though I did have a dangerous and frightening ectopic pregnancy a few years later when trying for my second — most likely due to scar tissue from the old surgery — I ultimately ended up having three children which is a miracle, and also, a little insane. My body, once a disintegrating and diseased lump of organs, had made so much life! Never mind years of yoga and pilates, finally, I felt strong. And even, a little bit beautiful.

Judy has a BA in the History of Science from Harvard, a PhD from the University of London, and has worked as a museum curator and university lecturer. She lives in New York City with her husband and three children.

Margaret McFarland and the Science of 'Mister Rogers' Neighborhood'

📅 31 Jul 2025 | ⏱️ 4 min read (886 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fatherly

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This modest developmental psychologist taught Mister Rogers everything she knew — and then he passed it on to us.
  • Industry observers note that before Fred Rogers slipped on his shoes and a cardigan, he was a young theology student attending the University of Pittsburgh in the 1950s.
  • McFarland was already a large figure in child psychology before ever meeting Fred Rogers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This modest developmental psychologist taught Mister Rogers everything she knew — and then he passed it on to us.

Industry observers note that before Fred Rogers slipped on his shoes and a cardigan, he was a young theology student attending the University of Pittsburgh in the 1950s. There, he studied under developmental psychologist Margaret McFarland, who would end up inspiring, influencing, and actively molding Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood. To say the show would not have been without McFarland is an understatement. Over the course of three decades, Rogers and McFarland met to discuss psychology, upcoming scripts, songs, and of course, children, on a weekly and sometimes daily basis, and her wisdom is imprinted all over the neighborhood.

McFarland was already a large figure in child psychology before ever meeting Fred Rogers. After receiving her doctorate from Columbia and teaching in Melbourne, Australia, McFarland returned to Pittsburgh in 1953 and co-founded the Arsenal Family and Children’s Center with Dr. Benjamin Spock, famous for his studies on child development, and renowned psychologist Erik Erikson, known for coining the eight stages of development and the term “identity crisis.”.

Unlike Spock and Erikson, McFarland kept a very low profile throughout her career and wrote very little about her teaching philosophies outside of her dissertation and a single journal article on “development of motherliness.” But her legacy has lived on through her students, Rogers chief among them, and the core tenet of what she taught should sound familiar, even if their origin is not.

Recent findings suggest that when Fred first began his study of child development at Pitt, McFarland help him get in touch with his own childhood memories and feelings. When doing this, she would repeatedly use the phrase, “Anything human is mentionable, and anything mentionable is manageable.” Simply put, it is OK to experience hard feelings openly, and more importantly, when people do this, they find healthier ways to cope. This theme comes up over and over again in Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood, like when Mister Rogers taught kids about how to get mad without hurting anyone, and feel many other complex feelings. It made for a catchy song and a crucial lesson in emotional intelligence, but like many of Roger’s great ideas, it started with McFarland in the classroom.

In a 2003 interview with the National Endowment for the Humanities, David McCullough boiled down McFarland’s worldview: “What she taught, in essence, is that attitudes aren’t taught, they’re caught. If the attitude of the teacher toward the material is positive, enthusiastic, committed, and excited, the students get that.”.

Rogers recalled favorite examples of McFarland putting this into practice in Stuart Omans’ and Maurice O’Sullivan’s book, Shakespeare Plays the Classroom. She had a well-known sculptor from Carnegie Mellon University come to Arsenal but told him not to teach, but to simply be excited about clay in front of the kids.

“And that’s what he did. He came once a week for a whole term, sat with the 4- and 5-year-olds as they played, and he ‘loved’ his clay in front of them,” Rogers said. “The children caught his enthusiasm for it, and that’s what mattered. So, like most good things, ‘teaching’ has to do with honesty.”.

Industry observers note that mcFarland championed a teaching philosophy based on love and compassion. Her friend and colleague Rev. Douglas Nowicki remembers that, “For her, learning could only take place in the context of love. She believed that if a child doesn’t sense that the teacher cares for him or her, then that child will not be able to learn very much.”.

Recent findings suggest that love is perhaps one of the most important supporting characters in Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood, more than Mr. McFeely and Daniel Tiger. There were his many ways to say “I love you” and how he always let children watching know he liked them just the way they are, not the things they wear or the way you do their hair. But love may have fallen into the background or been eclipsed by King Friday if it hadn’t been for Margaret.

Sources indicate that pittsburgh play therapist Carole McNamee, one of McFarland’s students, credits her with being one of the sharpest observers. “She could just spot things. She was phenomenal that way,” McNamee shared on the podcast When Fred Met Margaret.

“I’ve never seen anything like it before or since,” Margaret Mary Kimmel, a Ph.D. professor emerita of library and information sciences at Pitt, agreed. Kimmel eventually became a consultant for Mister Rogers and taught a class called Early Childhood and Media, which McFarland helped teach and develop material for. “Margaret talked about how the child interacted with the mother. ‘Did you see her face and the baby’s face? And what about when he started to fuss? How did the mother handle it?’ I learned so much from just watching her watch and describe to the class what was going on between the mother and the baby.”.

In a recent development, fred Rogers may have been the star of the show, but he never wavers from letting children be the center of attention. Even though he cannot see the kids watching at home, his gentle delivery and purposeful pauses helped them feel seen anyway.

What Gut Health Actually Means, In A World Where The Algorithm Is Constantly Shilling Supplements

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1124 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scarymommy

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Here’s what experts actually look for, recommend, and see as red flags.
  • Sources indicate that nervous system regulation, sleepmaxxing, high-functioning burnout — there is always some hot new health topic du jour.
  • We’ve heard the term; what does it actually mean?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Here’s what experts actually look for, recommend, and see as red flags.

Sources indicate that nervous system regulation, sleepmaxxing, high-functioning burnout — there is always some hot new health topic du jour. While there’s usually some kernel of true health information buried in the hype, it’s hard to parse what really matters from all the social media “gurus” shilling supplements at the link in bio. This is especially true of “gut health,” a topic that feels like it has dominated wellness spaces for the past few years but also never really comes up in your primary care doctor’s office. So, what does gut health actually mean, particularly for women? What do we need to know, and what is social media fluff?

We’ve heard the term; what does it actually mean? In general, gut health refers to the state of your gastrointestinal tract and how it’s working for you, according to the American Medical Association (AMA). Regular bowel movements, no persistent pain or bloating — these are signs things are going well. Medically speaking, good gut health doesn’t mean you’ve somehow optimized your microbiome (more on that in a minute); it means your digestive tract is functioning as it should, you’re absorbing the nutrients you need, and you’re comfortable throughout the process.

“I think that it looks different for everybody, but when I have a healthy gut, I feel better overall in my day-to-day life. It’s no bloating on a consistent basis. It’s having regular bowel movements. I’m not racing to the bathroom with loose stools or, on the other side of it, I’m not going days constipated. I don’t feel that brain fog. I have energy, and I’m sleeping well,” notes Chloe Melas, NBC News correspondent and author of The Girl’s Guide to Guts, who lives with ulcerative colitis, a type of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD).

Yes, it is a real thing and the subject of reams of medical research.

According to recent reports, inside your intestines live trillions of microorganisms that have a surprising impact on our overall health. According to The Cleveland Clinic, they help break down our food, support our immune systems, and may even play a role in mood and behavioral health. There’s no one perfect gut microbiome either, according to the AMA. Each person’s is unique and depends on their age, diet, medications, genetics, where they live, and more.

It’s normal to have an off tummy day every now and then, sure, but from her own experience and speaking with experts while writing her book, Melas knows there are certain red flags women should watch for when it comes to their gut health.

In a recent development, “If you’re having blood in your stool on a consistent basis, and that more than a handful of times, you need to go see a doctor immediately. That can look like going to see your primary care. Personally, in my experiences in writing this book and interviewing so many different experts, and just what I've gone through in my own life having IBD, I’d say go straight to a gastroenterologist,” Melas states.

Vomiting, unexplained weight loss, chronic stomach pain, and difficulty swallowing are also red flags, per the AMA. Inconsistent bowel movements, whether that means racing to the bathroom multiple times a day or being chronically constipated, are another reason to schedule an appointment with your doctor, she adds. Cramping, painful bloating, or looking pregnant after eating a meal — these things are not normal, says Melas.

Ignoring early signs of GI complications can keep you from feeling your best, and in some cases, missing a diagnosis you need. Women are twice as likely as men to have IBS, according to the American College of Gastroenterology.

In a recent development, “For so long, so many of us have just sort of been like, ‘This is just the way life is.’ I think that as women, we just don’t prioritize our health like we should, especially when it comes to our gut health. We’re really good about getting our mammograms and talking about our breast health. We are now finally talking about perimenopause and those symptoms. But 45 million Americans suffer from IBS. Nearly 4 million Americans suffer from inflammatory bowel disease, which raises your chances of having colon cancer. And these are things that require a doctor to help you diagnose.”.

In a recent development, probiotic sodas, gummies, powders... what do experts say will actually help improve your GI health and comfort? What will actually make your microbiome happy, and what’s not worth the money? Health experts agree that a diet rich in fiber is the best way to support your gut’s health.

“I had the privilege of interviewing Dr. William Lee, and he wrote a famous book called Eat to Beat Disease. He mentioned that you have 39 trillion different bacteria that live inside your microbiome and that you need this gut diversity to have overall good health, and that it really just comes down to having a diverse plate every day when you’re sitting down for your meals,” Melas says.

In a recent development, it’s generally recommended for adults to consume 25 to 30 grams of fiber per day, which Melas admits can be hard sometimes with diet alone. That may mean a fiber supplement is worth the investment for you, or it may mean snacking on more fruits and veggies throughout the day where you can.

“We all get so overwhelmed; we’re constantly being targeted by drink this, eat that, take this supplement, take these vitamins. But Dr. Lee states that really what you need is in the front of the grocery store. It's the fruits, it's the vegetables, and that it's the things that are easiest to reach first,” Melas adds.

Ultimately, Melas notes she wants more women to prioritize their health, and not to be embarrassed or afraid to talk to their providers about GI health specifically.

In a recent development, “If you are not having regular bowel movements, and by that I mean a big, beautiful, healthy poop every single day, then something is off with your gut health, full stop, and you need to get it figured out,” she states. “If you are bloated all the time, if you feel like every time you eat that cheese or a certain meal that you all of a sudden look like you’re three months pregnant, you’re not imagining it and you’re not crazy. We’ve just been told for so long to normalize it, and it's embarrassing, and it's not sexy, and who wants to sit around with your girlfriends at night and talk about the consistency of your stools? But we need to be talking about it because, honestly, it could save lives.”.

#137394. Essentials You Need To Know About Internet Safety For Kids
